sections.title: Section A: Evolution by Natural Selection (Finch Beak Depth Data)
sections.instructions: Answer all questions in this section. Refer to Figure 1 (Finch beak depth data table and graph) to answer the questions.
sections.stimulus:
Figure 1: Finch beak depth data table and graph showing environmental changes and morphological adaptations over a four-year period:
- 2019: rainfall 820 mm, hard seeds 24%, mean beak depth 8.7 mm
- 2020: rainfall 610 mm, hard seeds 37%, mean beak depth 9.1 mm
- 2021: rainfall 430 mm, hard seeds 58%, mean beak depth 9.8 mm
- 2022: rainfall 390 mm, hard seeds 64%, mean beak depth 10.2 mm

questions.question: Calculate the difference in mean beak depth (in mm) of the finches between the years 2019 and 2022. Show all your working.
memo: 10.2 mm - 8.7 mm (1 mark for correct values from table)
= 1.5 (1 mark for correct calculation)
mm (1 mark for correct unit)

questions.question: Describe the trend in rainfall and the availability of hard seeds from 2019 to 2022 as shown in Figure 1.
memo: Rainfall decreased consistently over the four-year period from 820 mm to 390 mm. (2 marks)
The percentage of hard seeds increased consistently over the same period from 24% to 64%. (2 marks)

questions.question: Explain how the change in rainfall from 2019 to 2022 acted as a selection pressure favoring finches with larger beak depths.
memo: A decrease in rainfall (drought conditions) reduced the availability of soft seeds. (2 marks)
This left hard seeds as the primary available food source (increasing from 24% to 64%). (2 marks)
Finches with larger beak depths were better adapted to crack open and feed on these hard seeds, giving them a survival advantage over those with smaller beaks. (2 marks)

questions.question: Using Darwin's theory of natural selection, explain why a larger mean beak depth became more common in this finch population over the four-year period.
memo: There is variation in beak depth within the finch population. (1 mark)
Some finches had larger beak depths, while others had smaller beak depths. (1 mark)
The environmental change (decreased rainfall/increased hard seeds) acted as a selection pressure. (1 mark)
Finches with larger beak depths had a favorable adaptation to feed on the hard seeds. (1 mark)
These finches survived the drought conditions (survival of the fittest). (1 mark)
Finches with smaller beak depths could not feed efficiently and died. (1 mark)
The surviving finches reproduced and passed on the allele/gene for larger beak depth to their offspring. (1 mark)
Over generations, the frequency of the allele for larger beak depth increased, making it more common in the population. (1 mark)

questions.question: State TWO environmental factors, other than rainfall, that could influence food availability for finches in an ecosystem.
memo: Temperature fluctuations (affecting plant growth). (2 marks)
Interspecific competition (other species feeding on the same seeds). (2 marks)
Accept: Disease affecting seed-producing plants / Human habitat destruction. (Any 2 factors, 2 marks each)

sections.title: Section B: Scientific Investigation Design
sections.instructions: Answer all questions in this section. Refer to Figure 2 (Investigation method and data sheet) to critique and evaluate the scientific design.
sections.stimulus: Figure 2: Investigation method and data sheet. A group of learners designed an investigation to test how seed hardness affects the survival rate of finches with different beak sizes. They recorded their observations on a data sheet but need to evaluate the quality of their scientific method.

questions.question: Formulate a suitable hypothesis for this investigation based on the relationship between seed hardness and finch beak depth.
memo: Finches with larger beak depths will have a higher survival rate when only hard seeds are available compared to finches with smaller beak depths. (3 marks)
Award 3 marks if both variables (seed hardness/beak depth and survival rate) are present, it shows a clear relationship, and is testable. Award 1-2 marks if partially correct.

questions.question: Identify the independent and dependent variables in this investigation.
memo: Independent variable: Seed hardness / percentage of hard seeds. (2 marks)
Dependent variable: Survival rate of finches / mean beak depth of surviving finches. (2 marks)

questions.question: State THREE variables that must be controlled (kept constant) during this investigation to ensure a valid test.
memo: The species of finches used in the trials. (2 marks)
The environmental conditions (e.g., temperature, light, water availability). (2 marks)
The duration of the feeding trial/exposure to the seeds. (2 marks)
Accept: The total amount of seeds provided daily. (Any 3, 2 marks each)

questions.question: Explain the difference between the reliability and the validity of this scientific investigation.
memo: Reliability refers to the consistency of the results, which can be improved by repeating the experiment or using a larger sample size. (2 marks)
Validity refers to whether the experiment is testing what it claims to test, which is achieved by controlling all variables except the independent variable. (2 marks)

questions.question: Critique the method quality of this investigation if the learners only used 5 finches in a single trial. Suggest how they can improve the reliability of their results.
memo: Critique: A sample size of 5 finches is too small to represent the population and makes the results highly susceptible to individual anomalies/unreliable. (2 marks)
Improvement: Increase the sample size (e.g., use 100 finches) and repeat the entire investigation multiple times to calculate an average. (2 marks)

questions.question: Based on the data provided in Figure 1, write a scientifically sound conclusion that the learners could record on their data sheet regarding the relationship between hard seed percentage and mean beak depth.
memo: An increase in the percentage of hard seeds in the environment leads to an increase in the mean beak depth of the surviving finch population. (4 marks)
Award 4 marks for a complete statement linking the independent variable (hard seeds) to the evolutionary outcome (mean beak depth) with correct directionality.

sections.title: Section C: Human Evolution Evidence and Interpretation
sections.instructions: Answer all questions in this section. Refer to Figure 3 (Hominin skull comparison diagram) to compare anatomical features and explain evolutionary changes.
sections.stimulus: Figure 3: Hominin skull comparison diagram showing Skull A (representing an earlier hominin profile) and Skull B (representing a later hominin profile). Label A indicates cranial capacity, Label B indicates jaw projection, and Label C indicates the position of the foramen magnum.

questions.question: Identify the anatomical features represented by Labels A, B, and C in Figure 3.
memo: Label A: Cranial capacity / brain size. (1 mark)
Label B: Jaw projection / prognathism. (1 mark)
Label C: Foramen magnum position. (1 mark)

questions.question: Compare the cranial capacity (Label A) of Skull A with Skull B, and explain the evolutionary significance of this change for hominins.
memo: Comparison: Skull A has a smaller cranial capacity than Skull B. (2 marks)
Significance: An increased cranial capacity indicates a larger brain size. (2 marks)
This allowed for higher cognitive functions, such as complex tool-making, language development, and social coordination. (2 marks)

questions.question: Describe the difference in jaw projection (Label B) between Skull A and Skull B, and explain how this change is linked to dietary shifts in human evolution.
memo: Difference: Skull A is highly prognathous (protruding jaw), whereas Skull B is orthognathous (flatter, more vertical face). (2 marks)
Dietary link: Earlier hominins (Skull A) consumed raw, tough vegetation and meat, requiring large jaws and strong chewing muscles. (2 marks)
Later hominins (Skull B) began cooking food (using fire), which softened the diet and reduced the selection pressure for large jaws and teeth. (2 marks)

questions.question: Explain how the position of the foramen magnum (Label C) differs between Skull A and Skull B, and how this anatomical change supports bipedalism.
memo: Difference: In Skull A, the foramen magnum is positioned towards the back (posteriorly), while in Skull B, it is positioned centrally/ventrally at the base of the skull. (2 marks)
Support for bipedalism: A central foramen magnum allows the head to balance vertically on top of the vertebral column. (2 marks)
This reduces the muscular effort needed to keep the head upright, which is a key adaptation for bipedal locomotion. (2 marks)

questions.question: State TWO skeletal adaptations, other than skull features, that provide evidence for bipedalism in hominins.
memo: An S-shaped vertebral column (spine) to absorb shock and keep the center of gravity over the pelvis. (2 marks)
A short, wide, bowl-shaped pelvis to support the upper body weight. (2 marks)
Accept: A carrying angle of the femur (knees angled inwards) / Non-opposable big toe aligned with other toes. (Any 2, 2 marks each)

rubric.criterion: Section A: Evolution by Natural Selection
rubric.descriptor: Measures the learner's ability to calculate changes, describe trends, link environmental factors to selection pressures, and apply Darwin's theory of natural selection to data.
Measures the learner's ability to formulate hypotheses, identify variables, critique experimental methods, distinguish reliability from validity, and draw conclusions.

Measures the learner's ability to identify hominin skull features, compare anatomical structures, and explain the evolutionary significance of changes in cranial capacity, jaw projection, and bipedalism.
